questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I picked Barcelona specifically because of the city and the culture. I love Spain and wanted somewhere with nice weather, potential for a good social life and a place to practice my spanish.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The school was very different from back home and not the best in my opinion, but the city, the vibe, the social life, the people, the food, the weather and the nightlife was all fantastic!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I think going on exchange in general takes a bit of effort and requires a lot of time with figuring stuff out. On top of that, Universitat de Barcelona is very old school with a lot of stuff still not being digitalized. The Spanish culture is always a bit late and laid back, so you had to do a lot on your own to get the necessary information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: We had a check in at school and it worked ok. Of course there is always a bit of chaos moving to a new place and a new university, but everything worked out and there were people who could help you if you needed it.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: A bit late at giving information and not always too organized, but everything worked out fine.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I got a specific place recommended through a friend from back home, but there are some platforms that can help you find acommodation - idealista was specifically popular (all my roommates found the place through idealista).

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Come down here and maybe rent an airbnb/hostel for some days while you go on idealista and go out and visit places. I highly recommend finding a place with other exchange students/young people. I lived with 12 other people and it was a fantastic way to get friends and get to know new people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I dont think there is a lot to find through the university but it seemed like there was quite a lot available through private apps, platforms etc.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: A bit weird and very different from back home - but everything worked out.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You get a HUGE course catalog with available courses and then you have to pick courses that are relevant for you and get them approved by KU (Home university). Then some time in July/August, Universitat de Barcelona open for a link, where you have to be ready to get the courses you want. You have to spend a lot of time to be ready for this because you need to make sure that neither the classes or the exams overlaps with some of the other courses you choose.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: I had to take quite a lot of time to apply for the courses but there were both some people at my home university and UB that could help me. The only problem was that a lot of these people were on holiday for a lot of the summer, so it could take some time to get an answer.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I didn't get the classes I initially wanted because some of the lectures overlapped but I got the classes that I wanted which didn't overlap.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Do stuff in good time because it can be a bit difficult to get help in the middle of the summer when people are on holiday. Don't be too stressed about if everything doesn't go to plane or what not - everything will work out.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Differed a lot. In general I would say it was a bit lower level than back home.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
Very different from back home. It was a lot more like high school (gymnasium) where you had to, or were strongly incentivized to participate in class, do weekly/monthly assignments and participate in smaller exams or group projects throughout the semester. Besides from that, the school is very old school - exams are still written exams with pen and paper. 
The thing I found the most frustrating was the huge difference in level and structure from course to course. Some of the courses were super duper easy (pretty much everyone could get a top grade without even trying) and some other courses were very tough with a huge syllabus and required a lot of studying. The structure was pretty much up to the individual teacher in how they wanted to structure the lectures/classes and how they wanted to examine the students. I found this a bit frustrating, especially in the exam period, because you had to adapt to a lot of different exam structures and every exam had different requirements to pass.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
-Game Theory for Business (merit for Micro III) - it was super easy.
-Corporate Finance - very big syllabus but very interesting. 
-International Economics
-Strategic Management - very easy but I did not like it. 
-World Economic History

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend International Economics it was really interesting and we had a very good professor. I would also recommend corporate finance even though it required a lot of studying.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: If you really want to enjoy your life, the city and the surrounding cities/nature you will probably end up spending a lot of money, so have that in mind.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
- Museums, parks, trips etc. were more expensive than I expected.
- Housing was a bit more expensive than I expected - pretty much the same as in Denmark
- Food was a little bit more expensive than I expected compared to other parts of Spain that I have travelled a lot. You can feel that Barcelona is a big city and the prices are therefore also a big higher.
- Drinks is super cheap. At a restaurant/bar you can normally get a beer/soda at around 2-3 euros.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: They offered a lot of different stuff but I would have wished for some cafees/bar or some parties at the university - they didn't have any parties or anything like that arranged by the university or at the university.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer:
They had a lot of different culture/language activities as well as a lot of sports activities. I signed up for a spanish class which I got at a very favorable price (180 euros for 4 x 1,5 hour classes a week for 10 weeks = 60 hours. This was a lot cheaper than private classes and I got to do it with other exchange students at the same Spanish level as me). 
Furthermore, I signed up for padel tennis classes which were held at the school sports campus together with other students. It cost 90 euros for 16 hours of padel classes (which is extremely cheap for padel). 
The school had a sports campus only 10 minutes walk from my campus where you could get an annual membership for around 100 euros and then freely use the gym, swimming pool, football pitches, padel courts, tennis courts etc.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I recommend the spanish classes and the sports activities.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
Explore Barcelona and the surrounding nature. Go to museums, parks etc. Go to the beach when the weather is good. Explore and find the nicest bars and restaurants (there are a lot). Go to the bars and clubs at night. You will have an amazing time in Barca!
I also recommend doing either one-day trips to the cities nearby - I went to Sitges, Lloret del Mar and Montserrat and can recommend it. 
Finally, I strongly recommend to go visit other parts and cities of Spain. Specifically I will recommend Valencia, Sevilla and San Sebastian - they are some of the most cozy places I have been to. There is quite a lot of cheap and relatively fast options with public transport in Spain.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. I love the culture and the vibe of the city - felt home from the start.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer:
I very highly recommend living with other students/young people. I lived in an apartment with 12 other young people from all over the world and it was the best decision! 
Because I found a lot of friends at my apartment and I got to know a few people from my classes as well, I didn't feel the big need to go to a lot of Erasmus events, but these events and trips that is organized every week is a very good way to meet friends and get to know a lot of other exchange students.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: In Spain it can be difficult with the language because they are not always very good at English, but I didn't see it as a huge problem. I only speak a very basic level of Spanish and therefore of course you miss out on some interaction with the local population, but I actually found that a lot of the local students wanted to practice their English and interact with foreign students.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Pretty much everything. I love their laid back attitude and the way they just chill on the street, in bars and restaurants all night. I love the language and the food as well. Don't settle for mediocre turistic tapas that you will find in other parts of Spain. Barcelona has some incredible and yet affordable restaurants and tapas bars.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
- Live with other students/young people - it is the easiest way to get to know people and make friends. If not, then make an effort to go to Erasmus events or approach people in class. All the exchange students are in similar situations and everybody is very open and nice and wants to make friends. Nobody goes on exchange and then don't want to meet new people.
- Be open minded about school - it is going to be very different from back home, and the application process might be a bit slow and tough, but everything will work out. 
- Go explore the city and the surrounding area in the weekends and on your day off - there is loads to see and enjoy!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
- Use idealista to find accommodation. 
- I would recommend learning just some basic Spanish before coming here - it just makes everything much more interesting and easy, and the locals really appreciate when you just try to speak Spanish.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The experiences and the friends that I got. I would not change my experience for anything. I can highly recommend going!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: - Trying to be as open-minded as possible with meeting new people from all over the world and learning about their cultures.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Enjoy!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
